thread.title: Be Greedy When Others Are Fearful - Real Estate Edition

author: Jussi Askola
title: Be Greedy When Others Are Fearful - Real Estate Edition
text:
The last few weeks have been increasingly challenging to REIT investors. The market volatility has returned – causing REIT share prices to go up and down by unusually high amounts on a daily basis. A true roller-coaster as we like to call it.
Many of our REIT holdings have declined in value in the recent weeks, and yet, we see no reason to worry about these short-term price movements. Opposite of that, as we shared in our latest Trade Alert , we are using the recent market weakness to increase our positions while prices are opportunistic.
Source: HYL Trade Alert
Interestingly, while the REIT market is affected by growing volatility, the private real estate market has continued with its steady rise to the upside. Property prices keep on rising in this strong economy with growing NOI and steady cap rates:
Source: NAREIT
Most property sectors are higher today than at the start of the year. Leading the pack in terms of price appreciation and total returns we have Self-Storage, Industrial and Manufactured Housing – three sectors that we like to overweight as part of our diversified Real Estate Portfolio.
Our self-storage positions: Iron Mountain ( IRM ), Jernigan ( JCAP ) and Global Self Storage ( SELF ) Our industrial positions: Plymouth ( PLYM ), W.P Carey ( WPC ), Lexington ( LXP ) Our manufactured housing position: UMH Properties ( UMH )
Source: NAREIT
Because private real estate prices have kept on going up in times of REIT market volatility, we believe that REIT share prices are particularly inexpensive today. Many of our portfolio holdings continue to trade at substantial discounts to NAV and we are today increasing our positions with a long term investment horizon.
Is the Private Market Overheating? No. Price increases in commercial real estate become unsustainable if they continually exceed the growth of net operating income (NOI). Today, this is not the case as property fundamentals remain strong with demand outpacing supply in most property sectors – allowing landlords to keep raising rents and achieving NOI growth.
Rent growth of apartments, office, retail and industrial are all positive:
Source: NAREIT
The vacancy rate is also at a historically low level for most property sectors with a continued trend towards even lower rates.
Source: NAREIT
It is then not surprising that properties continue to appreciate. Most importantly, it is good to remember that while REIT prices may deviate from property prices in the short run, they are strongly co-integrated in the long run. This means that as long as property fundamentals remain strong, we are set for attractive total returns for years to come, regardless of the occasional REIT market sell-off.
Where are we in the Real Estate Cycle? November 2018 marked 10 years since the beginning of the current real estate cyclical bull market. Many argue today that stocks remain still overpriced and that we could be slowly approaching the end of the current business cycle.
Here it is important to keep in mind despite trading in the form of “stocks”, REITs are real estate investments. As such, t he primary drivers of returns for REITs come from the real estate market cycle, not the business cycle that drives returns for almost all other companies traded on stock exchanges.
It makes an important difference because the length of the typical real estate cycle is much longer than the average business cycle.
The complete real estate market cycle has historically had an average duration of about 18 years, and we have good data for the last three full real estate market cycles:
Source: NAREIT
It shows that compared to the two previous cycles, the current one remains very short in length and unimpressive in magnitude. To reach the historical averages, the real estate market would need to keep rising for another 7 years, and with much sharper annual appreciation.
Of course, the last real estate downcycle was extremely severe as it combined a financial crisis with overbuilding and extreme leverage. It took a full 41 months for the REIT market to fully recover before prices would get back to their expansion phase. Because of that, a more telling comparison is between returns during the expansion phases—that is, after investors had recovered fully from the downturn.
Brad Case notes that:
For investors in the 1970s and 80s, the expansion phase that ran 155 months from September 1976 through August 1989 gave them total returns averaging 18.7% per year. For investors in the 1990s and 2000s, the expansion phase that ran total 190 months from March 1991 through January 2007 gave them total returns averaging 15.8% per year. In comparison, today’s investors haven’t nearly reaped the same rewards that they would have ordinarily expected from a REIT market expansion:
For today’s investors, the expansion phase has run only a total of 61 months from July 2012 through August 2017 and given them total returns averaging “only” 9.7% per year. Don’t get me wrong, 9.7% is not bad, but that is still far from the 15-18% annual returns that we experienced in the two previous real estate expansion phases; and the length of the expansion phase is not even at half of the previous ones.
It leaves us optimist that (1) the current real estate cycle could still have a long way to go, and (2) the REIT market is set for solid gains in the coming years as it recovers from the currently negative market perception.
We are especially optimistic when you consider that REITs are today trading at historically low valuations.
Opportunistic Prices to Boost Performance Regardless of what valuation metrics you look at, all the evidence points out that REITs are relatively cheap today. On a cash flow multiple basis, Lazard noted in mid-November that REIT valuations have fallen a full turn below the long-term average of 16.5x FFO. Since then, share prices have fallen another 10%:
Source
Historically High Discounts to NAV
The current P/NAV also suggests that REITs are substantially undervalued at a ~10% average discount compared to a 2-3% long-term average premium.
Source
The average dividend yield of the REIT sector is also today at an 8-year high:
Moreover, this is just the “average” and as such, it includes many low yielding, potentially overvalued REITs. By hand-picking only undervalued high yielding REITs, our Core Portfolio yields a hefty 8.5%. From here, even with minimal growth we can target very attractive long term results.
The same cannot be said about the most large-cap stocks such as Amazon ( AMZN ), Facebook ( FB ), Alphabet ( GOOG ), or Netflix ( NFLX ) which rely on strong growth to continue generating attractive returns. Even Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) may be overpriced if sales of iPhones start dropping.
In comparison, REITs have significantly less optimism and growth priced into their share prices – providing greater margin of safety.
Take Aways: Property prices continue to go up in today’s economy, despite the recent volatility of the financial market. In the long run, REIT share prices closely follow the appreciation of the private market and even outperform it. We plan to use the short-term price weakness in REITs to increase positions to boost our long-term performance Not every REIT dropped to the same extent, and some are more opportunistic than others. Today is time to be very selective.
